title: Upakosala and the talking fires
hookLine: a student tends his teacher's fires for twelve years and is never sent home; then the fires themselves begin to teach
carry: the guru points you to the self within
last: THE BULL — THE WHOLE WORLD TEACHES BRAHMAN.

cards: Satyakama grows up and becomes a teacher himself, with a student of his own, Upakosala. For twelve years, Upakosala lives in his teacher's house and tends the sacred fires, morning and evening.
Other students come, finish and are sent home. Not him. Then Satyakama leaves on a journey, still without teaching him, and Upakosala, the text says, is so sad he stops eating.
The teacher's wife begs him to eat something. No, he says. I'm full of sorrow.
And that's when the fires he's tended for twelve years start to talk.

teach.b: The fires confer among themselves. This student has served us well; let's teach him. Together they tell him: breath is Brahman.
Ka is Brahman. Kha is Brahman. Upakosala is honest: I understand breath is Brahman, but not ka and kha.

teach.h: KA IS JOY. KHA IS SPACE.
teach.b: Ka means joy, they explain, and kha means space, and they're one: the joy that is also space, the space that is also joy.
Then each of the three fires teaches him about itself, and about the sun, the moon, the lightning, the waters. We've told you our part, they say. Your teacher will tell you the way.

When Satyakama comes home, he looks at his student and says what was said to him years ago: your face shines like someone who knows Brahman. Who taught you? Upakosala, a little embarrassed, glances at the fires.
Satyakama listens, then says: they told you about the worlds. I'll tell you the rest.
As water doesn't cling to a lotus leaf, wrongdoing doesn't cling to one who knows this.

teach.h: THE PERSON SEEN IN THE EYE.
teach.b: And his teaching is this: the person you see in the eye, that is the self, that is Brahman, deathless and fearless. The fires teach the outer things.
The teacher points inward, to the one looking out through the eyes. The story keeps both: Upakosala needed his teacher, and he needed the fires. This is the guru's job in Hindu life, then and now.
Not to pile up more facts about the world, but to turn you around, toward the self, the atman, the seer inside, and say: that is Brahman.

how: In the traditional guru-shishya relationship, a Hindu student serves and lives with a teacher for years; some Hindu traditions also speak of an inner guide, and of the outer teacher as one who points the student inward.

games.q: you're Upakosala. the fires have taught you about earth, sun, moon and lightning. your teacher comes home. where does he tell you to look next?
o: further out: the stars beyond the lightning.
inward: the person seen in the eye is the self, Brahman.
back to the fires, for a second round of lessons.
games.why: the fires taught the worlds. Satyakama turns him around: the seer inside, deathless and fearless, is Brahman.

practice: Light a diya or a candle if you have one, or look at any small light, and watch it for a few breaths: the flicker, the color. Then gently notice that someone is seeing it.
Don't try to find that someone; just rest in the fact of seeing, joy and space, ka and kha.

wordCard.voice: Upakosala, the student who tended the sacred fires for twelve years. The fires taught him about the world, and his teacher pointed him to the self within.

orig.note: Sanskrit ācārya: teacher. the fires tell Upakosala that his ācārya will show him the way.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: the guru points you to the self within. It's where Satyakama's teaching pointed. Day three hundred thirty-seven, done.
